entities.summary:
Matthew of Aquasparta (born Matthew Bentivenga), a distinguished Italian Friar Minor and scholastic philosopher, served as the Minister General of the Franciscan Order from 1287 to 1289 and was elevated to Cardinal by Pope Nicholas IV in 1288. Born in Aquasparta, Umbria, his intellectual contributions significantly shaped late 13th-century Franciscan thought, particularly through his staunch defense of Augustinian intellectualism against the rising tide of Thomistic Aristotelianism. His career spanned prominent academic roles at the Universities of Paris and Bologna, where he earned a reputation as a formidable theologian and master of the Sacred Page, placing him at the heart of the era's most profound philosophical and theological debates.

Matthew's academic career began with studies in Paris, where he likely became a master of theology by 1278. He subsequently taught at the Franciscan studium in Bologna before returning to Paris as a regent master in 1281. His election as Minister General of the Franciscan Order in 1287 marked a critical juncture, as he sought to steer the order through internal theological controversies and administer its vast network across Europe. Following his brief but impactful tenure, Pope Nicholas IV, himself a former Minister General of the Franciscans, appointed him Cardinal-Priest of San Lorenzo in Panisperna. As a cardinal, Matthew played an influential role in the papal curia, notably participating in the tumultuous papal conclaves of 1292–1294 that elected Celestine V and Boniface VIII, and served as a papal legate to France and England.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Matthew of Aquasparta significantly shaped late 13th-century Franciscan theology, solidifying an Augustinian intellectual tradition against Aristotelianism and influencing subsequent scholastic figures like Duns Scotus. His leadership as Minister General and cardinal also placed him at the center of critical ecclesiastical and political events.
